conversation.content:
Hi there, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure you’re supported in every way after having your baby.  

I’d like to use a short, well-trusted tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. Your answers are completely confidential, and there are no right or wrong responses—just whatever is true for you. When we’re done, we’ll talk about what the score might mean and what resources could help, if you’d like.  

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

1. Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Lately… not very often. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute video or if the baby does something silly, but it feels forced, like I’m doing it because I should, not because it comes naturally. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find things genuinely funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often… maybe once or twice in the past week. Even when something is clearly funny, it feels like I’m watching it through a fog. I’ll give a little smile, but the laughter doesn’t really bubble up the way it used to before the baby came.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly… hardly at all. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I’ll think “I should want to do this,” but the enjoyment part just isn’t there. I still go through the motions, mostly so people won’t worry, but the looking-forward feeling is pretty much gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I’m not holding him the “right” way or my milk isn’t good enough. When I dropped the pacifier on the floor yesterday, I told myself I was a terrible mom for not keeping everything perfectly clean. Even little stuff, like forgetting to bring a burp cloth to the couch, turns into “I’m failing at this.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yes. Even when everything looks fine on the outside, my stomach’s still in knots. I’ll sit there watching the baby sleep, convinced something’s wrong—maybe he’s too quiet, maybe his breathing changed, maybe I missed a sign. I check that the monitor is on five times an hour. There’s no real reason, but the worry just parks itself in my chest and won’t leave.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and I have to grip the couch cushion so I don’t jump up and pace. Nothing’s happening, the baby’s fine, but my body acts like an alarm went off. It passes after ten or fifteen minutes, but it leaves me exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… quite a lot. Some days it feels like the second one feeding ends, the laundry pile or the dishes or the next diaper change is already staring at me. I’ll be rocking the baby and thinking, “How am I going to get through the rest of today, let alone tomorrow?” I haven’t fallen apart, but it’s that constant sense that I’m barely treading water and the next wave could come any minute.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. Even when the baby’s finally down, my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles right, am I producing enough milk, will he wake up in an hour? I lie there staring at the ceiling, and if I do drift off, I jolt awake at every tiny sound. A couple of nights this week I’ve been awake until three, just stuck in that sad, wired loop.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a heavy blanket I can’t push off. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead there’s this steady ache in my chest. Sometimes I cry, sometimes I just sit there feeling empty. It’s not constant crying anymore, but the sadness is always humming in the background.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times—maybe three nights this week. It’s usually after I’ve finally got the baby down and the house is quiet. All the little worries pile up, and I’ll just sit on the couch with tears leaking out, thinking I’m failing him somehow. The crying doesn’t last long, maybe ten minutes, but it leaves me drained.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never imagined hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom to my baby.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels distant, replaced by a fog of worry, self-criticism, and exhaustion. Laughing now feels mechanical, plans feel like chores, and each day seems to be "treading water" while a steady ache of sadness hums in the background. Your courage in describing these feelings shows deep care for your baby and a strong wish to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response describes markedly reduced ability to laugh and enjoy humor, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>The patient explicitly states "hardly at all" and describes complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty much every day" for multiple minor events, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, near-daily worry without cause, constant physical tension, and intrusive thoughts—aligns with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete panic-like episodes this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping ('barely treading water'), matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts and frequent awakenings, consistent with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily sadness, emotional heaviness, and an unshakeable ache—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 22 (items 3,5-10 reversed) exceeds the 14-point threshold for probable major postpartum depression, supported by <sym>markedly reduced pleasure</sym>, pervasive self-blame, nightly ruminative insomnia, frequent overwhelm, and discrete panic attacks. These align with core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartonset</med>: depressed mood most days, diminished interest, fatigue, guilt, sleep disturbance, and anxiety. No self-harm ideation reduces immediate safety risk but does not lessen clinical urgency. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Discuss evidence-based options: individual <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and consider antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Encourage 20-30 min outdoor daylight walks and acceptance of help with night feeds to improve sleep hygiene
4. Share local hotlines (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) for 24/7 emotional support
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS format)

1. Anhedonia: marked reduction in ability to laugh/feel pleasure; “watching through a fog.”  
2. Loss of anticipatory enjoyment: daily activities feel like chores; no “looking-forward” feeling.  
3. Excessive guilt/self-blame: daily rumination about being a “terrible mom” over minor events.  
4. Generalized anxiety: near-daily worry, “knots in stomach,” repeated safety-checking behaviors.  
5. Panic episodes: 2–3/week, sudden racing heart/shakiness without trigger, resolves 10-15 min.  
6. Perceived inability to cope: frequent sense of “treading water,” overwhelmed by routine tasks.  
7. Mood-linked insomnia: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep even when infant sleeps; ruminative worry.  
8. Persistent sad mood: “heavy blanket,” daily background ache, occasional tearfulness.  
9. Crying spells: 3× this week, situational, brief but exhausting.  
10. Self-harm ideation: denied (“No… I just want to feel like me again”).

Pattern: Consistent with moderate-to-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms arising postpartum.  
Risk factors: anhedonia, guilt cognitions, sleep disruption, panic symptoms, impaired coping.  
Safety: no self-harm or suicidal thoughts reported; no plan/intent.

Screening significance: elevated likelihood of major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; referral for comprehensive clinical assessment and follow-up recommended.
